video_goal: Visually demonstrate how to determine the gender of a Red-Eared Slider turtle by examining its claws, tail, cloaca, and plastron.
required_subjects_and_props: Male Red-Eared Slider turtle, Female Red-Eared Slider turtle, shallow water enclosure, blunt pointer tool, small straight-edge ruler

outline_steps.visual_action: Hands gently lift a Red-Eared Slider turtle from a shallow water enclosure, rotating it slightly to reveal the distinctive red stripe behind its eye.
Hands hold the turtle facing the camera, using a thumb and forefinger to gently extend one of the turtle's front legs outward.
A blunt pointer tool taps the exceptionally long, curved front claws of the male turtle, then taps the short, stubby front claws of a female turtle shown in a side-by-side visual.
Hands gently rotate the turtle 180 degrees to face away from the camera, exposing the posterior end and tail.
Fingers gently lift the male turtle's tail, highlighting its thick base and long length extending well past the edge of the back shell.
Fingers lift a female turtle's tail, demonstrating its noticeably shorter length and thinner base tucked closer to the shell.
The blunt pointer tool indicates the cloaca opening on the underside of the male's tail, showing it is positioned far down the tail, past the edge of the upper shell.
The pointer tool indicates the cloaca opening on the female's tail, showing it is positioned much closer to the body, underneath the edge of the upper shell.
Hands gently flip the male turtle upside down, supporting its carapace (top shell) in the palm to fully expose the plastron (bottom shell).
A small straight-edge ruler is placed flat across the center of the male turtle's plastron, revealing a visible gap underneath the ruler that indicates a concave shape.
The straight-edge ruler is placed across the center of the female turtle's plastron, showing the ruler resting completely flush against the flat shell with no gap.
Hands gently turn the turtle right-side up and slowly lower it back into the shallow water enclosure until it swims away.
